segments.t: Opening branches right beside police stations soon brings Detective Mori of the Hokkaido Police through the door. While Mori inspects the stock for rule violations, Muranishi answers every complaint with unshakable politeness. Listen to the Japanese confrontation first without worrying about catching every word.
どうされました？
道警の森だ。責任者はいるか？
会長、警察の方が来ました。
どうしましたか？
警察の近くにばかり出しやがって。
一番近いところに出店したまでです。
この部分をよく見ろ。
ちゃんと規定をクリアしてますね。
違う！よく見ろ。
今日のところは勘弁してやる。
お前らの顔は覚えたからな。
どうぞお持ち帰りください。
Listen to the sharp contrast in register: Mori barks blunt commands while Muranishi treats him like an honored guest. Let's break down their lines.
どうされました？
'How may I help you?' "Dou saremashita" is a respectful upgrade of "dou shimashita", asking a customer or visitor what happened or what they need.
道警の森だ。
'I am Mori from the Hokkaido Police.' "Doukei" squeezes "Hokkaidou Keisatsu", Hokkaido Police, into a snappy two-part abbreviation.
責任者はいるか？
'Is the person in charge here?' "Sekininsha" joins "sekinin", responsibility, with "sha", person—the manager or person accountable.
会長、警察の方が来ました。
'Chairman, someone from the police has arrived.' Rather than saying "hito", person, Kitamori chooses respectful "kata" in "keisatsu no kata" to announce the officers politely.
警察の近くにばかり出しやがって。
'Opening shops right near the police stations, of all places.' "Bakari" means 'nothing but' or 'only', complaining that every branch pops up right next to "keisatsu", the police.
一番近いところに出店したまでです。
'We simply opened at the closest spot.' "Ichiban chikai" means closest of all, and ending with "made desu" shrugs it off modestly as 'we merely did that and nothing more'.
この部分をよく見ろ。
'Look closely at this part.' "Bubun" means section or part, and "miro" is the blunt command form of "miru", to look—used by tough bosses or detectives, never with strangers in polite company.
違う！
'Wrong!' By itself, "chigau"—from the verb 'to differ'—is the everyday Japanese way to say 'no, that's wrong!' or 'not like that!'.
今日のところは勘弁してやる。
'I will let it slide for today.' "Kyou no tokoro wa" frames 'as far as today goes', and "kanben shite yaru" grants pardon from above with tough-guy "te yaru".
お前らの顔は覚えたからな。
'I have memorized your faces, understand?' "Omaera" is a rough plural 'you lot', while "kao", face, plus "oboeta", remembered, delivers a classic parting warning.
どうぞお持ち帰りください。

'Please feel free to take these home with you.' Wrapping "mochikaeri", takeout or carrying home, between "o" and "kudasai" sounds like a polite pastry shop—which makes Muranishi's parting shot hilarious. Now let's hear the whole inspection scene again.
どうされました？
道警の森だ。責任者はいるか？
会長、警察の方が来ました。
どうしましたか？
警察の近くにばかり出しやがって。
一番近いところに出店したまでです。
この部分をよく見ろ。
ちゃんと規定をクリアしてますね。
違う！よく見ろ。
今日のところは勘弁してやる。
お前らの顔は覚えたからな。
どうぞお持ち帰りください。
Notice how "douzo omochikaeri kudasai" is actually a helpful everyday expression you will see at bakeries and restaurants for takeout, repurposed here with sly humor. See you next time.
また明日。
